Lessons.Title: Relate Area to Multiplication
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: establish the area of a rectangle having one positive whole-number side and a UNIT fractional side by counting and regrouping shaded parts. The 2021 source deliberately allows students to choose counting, rearranging, or multiplication before giving a formal rule.

Warm-up — Which One Doesn't Belong: the source shows A as a 6×1 rectangle, B as a 1×6 tiled rectangular array, C as a triangle of base 4 and height 3, and D as a 12×(1/2) rectangle. Each has area 6 square units under the usual interpretations, despite different representations. The existing candidate's five-unit description was incorrect; no single WODB reason is mandatory. Teacher must assess a student explanation.

Activity 1 — Find the Area: the FOUR original source diagrams have the SAME 6-unit length, with fractional heights 1, 1/2, 1/3 and 1/4. Their shaded areas are respectively 6, 3, 2 and 1 1/2 square units. Students count shaded sixths/halves/thirds/fourths of square units, group partial squares into wholes and explain the area of each one. The previous candidate used length eight and height 1/8, changing the original quantities and task progression.

Activity 2 — Draw Rectangles: on grid paper construct and label four rectangles measuring 1/2×1, 1/2×2, 1/2×3, and 1/2×4 units, then report areas 1/2, 1, 1 1/2 and 2 square units. The original final shaded picture partly hides squares: students must state which dimensions or full/partial unit counts are required before estimating its area, rather than invent an exact area from insufficient information. A separately authored 6×1/3 rectangle is optional practice, not a replacement for the source's four drawings and hidden-square reasoning.

Teacher assessment: first inspect how six fractional-height columns correspond to the unit area; recognize that the source warm-up includes a 4×3 triangle with area 6 rather than the former invented 5-unit examples. Drawings, rearrangements, estimating hidden unit counts and WODB argument remain teacher-scored. Source checked against public original 2021 teacher lesson/preparation and embedded Student Facing HTML. Separate original Student Task PDF, original asset rights and protected Cool-down NOT_VERIFIED.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit fractional width
KeyConcepts.Definition: One side length names one of b equal pieces of a linear unit.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For length a units and height 1/b unit, area is a×(1/b) square units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rearranging fractional unit squares
KeyConcepts.Definition: Shaded congruent strips can be collected into full squares without changing covered area.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Six 1/3-unit-square pieces can make two unit squares.
KeyConcepts.Example: 6 thirds of a square equal 2 squares.

KeyConcepts.Title: Two area interpretations
KeyConcepts.Definition: A×(1/b) counts A narrow parts while (1/b)×A takes a fraction of a whole A-square-unit rectangle.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Both describe the same area if unit lengths and the shaded region match.
KeyConcepts.Example: One quarter of eight square units is two.

WorkedExamples.Title: Four source 6-unit rectangles
WorkedExamples.Question: Find area when a rectangle is 6 units long and has heights 1, 1/2, 1/3, or 1/4 unit.
WorkedExamples.Method: Count six equal width-one columns and group fractional square units, preserving the original source dimensions.
Steps: For height 1, all 6 full unit squares are shaded: area 6.
For height 1/2, six half-squares combine into 3 square units.
For height 1/3, six third-squares combine into 2 square units.
For height 1/4, six quarter-squares combine into 6/4=1 1/2 square units.
WorkedExamples.Check: Multiply the source length 6 by 1, 1/2, 1/3 and 1/4, respectively.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original grid-paper construction sequence
WorkedExamples.Question: Draw four rectangles with height 1/2 unit and lengths 1, 2, 3, 4 units. Find each area.
WorkedExamples.Method: Build separate exact half-square models with equal 1-unit horizontal columns.
Steps: A 1×1/2 rectangle has one half-square.
A 2×1/2 rectangle has two half-squares, making 1 square unit.
A 3×1/2 rectangle has three half-squares, or 1 1/2 square units.
A 4×1/2 rectangle has four half-squares, or 2 square units.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher verifies equal half-unit heights and lengths against the student's physical drawing.

WorkedExamples.Title: Why a partially concealed grid needs more information
WorkedExamples.Question: A shaded rectangular picture hides some unit squares. Can its exact shaded area be determined without knowing the full length, fractional height or number of hidden pieces?
WorkedExamples.Method: Distinguish observed area parts from unknown overall dimensions.
Steps: Record visible unit widths and known fractional part size.
Identify whether the number of covered, hidden, or offscreen fractional squares is given.
If the total count cannot be inferred, show different compatible dimensions and explain why different areas are possible.
Give an estimate only under explicit assumptions; request the missing measurement for an exact result.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Not necessarily; the required complete fractional-piece count or full dimensions must be justified.
WorkedExamples.Check: Reject a claimed exact source area based only on the visible shaded pieces.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Count shaded narrow strips as whole squares
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It confuses linear lengths, equal-area partitions, or square-area quantities.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Partition the full-unit square according to the denominator before counting.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It confuses linear lengths, equal-area partitions, or square-area quantities.
CommonMistakes.Correction: One fourth is smaller than one unit when the original unit remains fixed.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use 8×1/8 or invent the area of the hidden region as a source answer
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The actual four source rectangles use fixed six-unit lengths with 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 heights, and the hidden-square question asks learners to analyze needed information.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use 6, 3, 2, 6/4 square-unit answers for the four source figures; draw the 1/2-by-1,2,3,4 grid-paper examples and identify hidden dimensions before claiming an exact area.

SummaryPoints: Original WODB source A: 6×1 rectangle, B: 1×6 tiled rectangle, C: base-4 height-3 triangle, D: 12×1/2 rectangle; several comparisons are defensible.
Activity 1 uses SIX-unit rectangles of heights 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4; areas are 6, 3, 2 and 1 1/2 square units.
Activity 2 constructs 1/2×1, 1/2×2, 1/2×3, 1/2×4 on grid paper; their areas are 1/2, 1, 1 1/2 and 2.
The original hidden-shading prompt asks what measurements are needed and invites bounded estimates; do not invent a uniquely determined exact count.

Lessons.Title: Fractional Side Lengths Less Than 1
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: find and represent rectangular areas when the width is a NON-UNIT fraction less than one. The source moves from one fourth or one third to widths such as two thirds or three fourths and invites multiple decomposition strategies.

Warm-up — estimate a length-seven rectangle shaded to a height between one half and one. Infer that the shaded area is between three and a half and seven square units, not an exact value without a precise shaded height. Discuss why an estimate around five square units is plausible rather than pretending a unique source-image result.

Activity 1 — Rectangle With a Fractional Side Length: source diagrams each have length FOUR units with non-unit fraction widths 2/3, 3/4 and 3/5. Count shaded 1/3-, 1/4- or 1/5-square-unit pieces, 8, 12 and 12 respectively; the areas are 8/3 = 2 2/3, 12/4 = 3, and 12/5 = 2 2/5 square units. The second and third rectangles both have 12 shaded pieces but different total areas because the pieces differ in size. The former candidate's length-five 3/4 and 2/3 rectangles are optional extensions, not the original tasks.

Activity 2 — What Are the Side Lengths?: first infer the dimensions of the 3×2/3 shaded rectangle from the unlabeled pieces: area 3×2/3 = 2 square units. Then inspect source diagrams X (length 3, width 4/5, area 12/5) and Y (length 5, width 3/4, area 15/4). Of the five source expression cards, (3/4)×5 matches Y; 3×(3/5) matches neither; 3×4×(1/5) matches X; 4×(3/4) matches neither; 3×3×(1/4) matches neither. A matching expression must show dimensions and the shaded region correctly, not merely have familiar factors.

Teacher assessment: for source Activity 1 the teacher distinguishes 12 quarter-square units from 12 fifth-square units. For source Activity 2 teacher checks which expression maps to diagram X or Y, including negative matches; the source does not ask learners to compare the invented 5×2/3 with 5×3/4 as its main task. A standalone matching table supports teaching but exact drawing and explanations need teacher assessment. Public 2021 teacher lesson/preparation and Student Facing HTML inspected. Separate Student Task PDF, original image licensing, gated Cool-down and selected Practice NOT_VERIFIED.

KeyConcepts.Title: Non-unit fractional width
KeyConcepts.Definition: A side length such as 3/4 means three of four equally sized linear-unit parts.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A whole length times a non-unit fractional width gives area in square units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Repeated fractional area pieces
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each one-unit column contributes the same fraction of a unit square.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A columns of c/d square unit yield (a×c)/d square units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Area comparison with a fixed length
KeyConcepts.Definition: For equal positive whole-number lengths, greater width produces greater area.
KeyConcepts.Rule: If p>q>0 and length a>0, then ap>aq.

WorkedExamples.Title: First source rectangle 4×2/3
WorkedExamples.Question: A rectangular shaded region is four units by two thirds of a unit. Find the area.
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify eight 1/3-square-unit shaded pieces, then combine them.
Steps: Partition each of four unit columns into thirds.
Shade two thirds in every column: 4×2=8 small pieces.
Eight pieces of size 1/3 square unit make 8/3 = 2 2/3 square units.

WorkedExamples.Title: Same twelve pieces, different unit fractional areas
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare the source's 4×3/4 and 4×3/5 shaded rectangles.
WorkedExamples.Method: Count three shaded fractional-square pieces per each of four unit columns, but keep denominators distinct.
Steps: 4×3=12 shaded pieces for both rectangles.
In the first, every piece is 1/4 square unit: 12/4=3 square units.
In the second, every piece is 1/5 square unit: 12/5=2 2/5 square units.
Reject the claim that equal counts of unequal-sized pieces guarantee equal areas.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 3 versus 12/5 square units, respectively; the 1/4 pieces are larger.
WorkedExamples.Check: 4×3/4=3 and 4×3/5=12/5; their difference is 3/5 square unit.

WorkedExamples.Title: Match X and Y with the five original source expression cards
WorkedExamples.Question: X has dimensions 3×4/5, Y has 5×3/4. Match expressions 3/4×5, 3×3/5, 3×4×1/5, 4×3/4 and 3×3×1/4 to X, Y or neither.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use exact rational areas and the geometric meaning of each factor, not superficial matching of numerals.
Steps: 3/4×5 = 15/4 and represents Y's five length units with 3/4 height.
3×4×1/5 = 12/5 and represents 12 shaded fifth-square parts in X.
3×3/5 = 9/5, 4×3/4 = 3 and 3×3×1/4 = 9/4, so these three expressions match neither.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Y: 3/4×5. X: 3×4×1/5. The other three do not match either shaded region.
WorkedExamples.Check: Reject 3×3/5, 4×3/4 and 3×3×1/4 even if students claim similar factor symbols.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Count the numerator as an unscaled whole width
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It confuses linear lengths, equal-area partitions, or square-area quantities.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Each fractional strip has size 1/d of a unit, not one full unit.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Multiply a whole length by a fractional width and report linear units
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It confuses linear lengths, equal-area partitions, or square-area quantities.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Rectangular area is in square units; side lengths remain linear.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claim 12 shaded pieces in two different fraction grids imply the same area
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A quarter-square and a fifth-square do not have the same area; the source explicitly contrasts 12×1/4 with 12×1/5.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep denominator units: 12×1/4=3 square units and 12×1/5=12/5 square units.

SummaryPoints: Original Activity 1: 4×2/3=8/3, 4×3/4=3, 4×3/5=12/5 square units; two cases each have 12 pieces but different part sizes.
Original Activity 2 first rectangle: 3×2/3=2 square units; infer the dimensions from fractional pieces.
Source X is 3×4/5=12/5 and Y is 5×3/4=15/4 square units; of five cards, 3×4×1/5 maps to X and 3/4×5 maps to Y, while three cards map to neither.
Correct numeric products alone do not establish original picture correspondences; student diagrams and explanatory justifications require teacher review.

Lessons.Title: Fractional Side Lengths Greater Than 1 PLC Activity
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: find the area of a rectangle when one side length is a fraction or mixed number GREATER THAN one; connect the whole and fractional subregions to expressions using unit area. Distinguish an improper fraction from a mixed number.
Warm-up: inspect possible true/false equalities, such as 10÷3=10×(1/3) and the false statement 10÷3=10 1/3. Explain why 10/3 is 3 1/3, not 10 1/3, with an area or number-line model.

Activity 1: draw an original rectangle 4 units high and 3 2/3 units wide. Shade the 3-by-4 whole portion separately from the 2/3-by-4 portion. Compute 12+8/3=14 2/3 square units; show equivalent improper side width 11/3 and product (11/3)×4=44/3.

Activity 2: sort original expressions by whether they represent the modeled rectangle. 4×(3+2/3), 12+8/3 and 44/3 are equivalent, but 4×(3+3/2) is not. Require students to defend the matching area diagram and identify why the nonmatching expression changes the fractional width.

Assessment: the source calls for selecting every valid expression and explaining how the geometry supports each; a numeric yes/no is insufficient for the open proof. Teacher evaluates the drawn region, equality reasoning and partner explanations. No source image cards are reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Mixed fractional side lengths
KeyConcepts.Definition: A width above one may combine whole units and a part of a unit.
KeyConcepts.Rule: If width w+f, the area for height h is h×w+h×f.

KeyConcepts.Title: Improper fraction equivalence
KeyConcepts.Definition: An improper fraction describes the same distance or area as an appropriately regrouped mixed number.

KeyConcepts.Title: Distributive rectangle
KeyConcepts.Definition: A split along one direction gives nonoverlapping rectangular subregions whose areas add.

WorkedExamples.Title: Area with width above one
WorkedExamples.Question: Find area of a rectangle 4 high and 3 2/3 wide.
WorkedExamples.Method: Build an original unit-area model, then justify the arithmetic.
Steps: Separate the 3-unit-wide region from the remaining 2/3-unit strip.
The first subarea is 4×3=12 square units.
The fractional subarea is 4×2/3=8/3; add to get 44/3.

WorkedExamples.Title: Match expressions to area
WorkedExamples.Question: Which expressions match a 4-by-3 2/3 rectangle?
WorkedExamples.Method: Build an original unit-area model, then justify the arithmetic.
Steps: Write 4×(3 2/3) and convert width to 11/3.
Compare 4×(3+3/2), whose width equals 4 1/2 instead.
WorkedExamples.Check: The rejected expression is 18 square units, different from 14 2/3.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject a mixed-number notation error
WorkedExamples.Question: Is 10÷3 equal to 10 1/3?
WorkedExamples.Method: Build an original unit-area model, then justify the arithmetic.
Steps: Divide ten into three equal groups to obtain 10/3.
Group nine thirds into three wholes, leaving 1/3.
Compare 3 1/3 with 10 1/3.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Read 10/3 as ten and one third
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It confuses linear lengths, equal-area partitions, or square-area quantities.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Group the numerator into complete groups of the denominator.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Forget the fractional strip when computing rectangular area
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It confuses linear lengths, equal-area partitions, or square-area quantities.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Split the entire mixed-length side and include both whole and fractional regions.

SummaryPoints: An area diagram can support a whole-times-mixed-number product.
Equivalent improper and mixed numbers produce the same exact area.
Matching and defending expressions and diagrams requires teacher review.

Lessons.Title: Decompose Area
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: compare two differently shaped rectangular gardens with mixed-number lengths, using equal-area decompositions and mathematical argument. The source explicitly asks which of two gardens has the greater area, not merely to find two disconnected products.
Warm-up: calculate a mixed-number product by splitting the mixed number, such as 5×(2+1/2)=10+2 1/2. Explain why adding two partial products corresponds to two nonoverlapping subrectangles.

Activity 1: in an original garden scenario, Elena designs a 4-by-6 1/2-yard garden and Mateo designs a 5-by-5 1/4-yard garden. Use grids to show Elena's 24+2=26 square yards, and Mateo's 25+1 1/4=26 1/4 square yards. Explain why Mateo's is bigger by a quarter square yard, even though Elena's longest side is longer.

Activity 2: draw each garden, label whole-unit and fractional subrectangles, exchange diagrams with a partner and critique whether every length and product matches. Describe how different decompositions can have equal totals; include nonvisual text area parts alongside student drawings.

Teacher review: the original Noah/Priya comparison with mixed lengths is a class discussion and written-revision task; the first-party replacement uses different numbers to avoid reproducing publisher student illustrations. The verdict and the exact diagram-derived justification must both be checked.

KeyConcepts.Title: Mixed-number decomposition
KeyConcepts.Definition: A side such as 6 1/2 units can be split into 6 and 1/2.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compare garden areas
KeyConcepts.Definition: The larger single side does not alone determine which rectangle has greater area.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compute or estimate both products with matching square units.

KeyConcepts.Title: A diagram supports a sum of subareas
KeyConcepts.Definition: When a rectangle is split into pieces without overlap, the original area is the sum of the pieces.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Every part must have corresponding valid side lengths.

WorkedExamples.Title: Elena's garden
WorkedExamples.Question: Elena's garden is 4 yards by 6 1/2 yards. Find its area.
WorkedExamples.Method: Build an original unit-area model, then justify the arithmetic.
Steps: Draw a 4×6 whole-number region and a 4×1/2 strip.
Calculate 4×6=24 square yards.
Calculate 4×1/2=2 and add.

WorkedExamples.Title: Mateo's garden
WorkedExamples.Question: Mateo's garden is 5 yards by 5 1/4 yards. Find its area.
WorkedExamples.Method: Build an original unit-area model, then justify the arithmetic.
Steps: Draw a 5×5 region and an adjoining 5×1/4 strip.
Find 25 square yards for the square region.
Add 5/4=1 1/4 square yards.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare both gardens
WorkedExamples.Question: Which garden is larger, and by how much?
WorkedExamples.Method: Build an original unit-area model, then justify the arithmetic.
Steps: Verify Elena's area is 26 square yards.
Verify Mateo's is 26 1/4 square yards.
Subtract 26 1/4−26 and explain the result geometrically.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Mateo's garden is larger by 1/4 square yard.
WorkedExamples.Check: A longer side does not necessarily give a larger rectangular area.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume the garden with the longest single side has greatest area
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It confuses linear lengths, equal-area partitions, or square-area quantities.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Area depends on the product of BOTH perpendicular side lengths.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Count a fractional strip as one whole extra strip
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It confuses linear lengths, equal-area partitions, or square-area quantities.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Multiply the fractional length by the other full dimension before adding.

SummaryPoints: A mixed-number side can be decomposed into whole and fractional strips.
Compare complete areas using square units before declaring a larger garden.
Garden drawings and revised comparisons are teacher-reviewed.

Lessons.Title: Area and Properties of Operations
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: match decomposed shaded area diagrams with different algebraic expressions and explain both adding a fractional subrectangle and subtracting an unshaded strip from a larger rectangle. The source uses a partner card sort with multiple valid matches, so a single expression cannot certify the discussion.
Warm-up: compare 4×(6+1/3) with 4×6+4×1/3, then contrast the related subtraction 4×6−4×1/3. Explain that parentheses and the plus/minus sign identify which regions are shaded.

Activity 1: construct two original rectangles with height 4. Rectangle A has 2 3/4 units shaded width, so its area is 4×(2+3/4)=8+3=11 square units. Rectangle B has a 3-unit bounding width but one quarter-unit strip left unshaded, so its shaded area is 4×3−4×1/4=12−1=11. Make separate area text diagrams; do not imply that the two differently positioned shaded regions are identical in shape.

Activity 2: give a partner expression cards containing 4×(2 3/4), 4×3−4×1/4, 12−1, and 4×(2+1/4). Ask which cards match which original diagrams and require an explanation of the different shaded regions. The last expression represents only 9 square units and does not match either 11-square-unit rectangle.

Assessment: the source asks students to match card diagrams with more than one expression and then write new equivalent expressions, using area subregions for proof. Since a correct matching number is not proof of a valid diagram, the card-sort matching, writing and oral reasoning require teacher review.

KeyConcepts.Title: Addition decomposition
KeyConcepts.Definition: Adjacent disjoint shaded rectangular pieces have total area equal to their summed areas.

KeyConcepts.Title: Subtraction decomposition
KeyConcepts.Definition: A shaded rectangle may be the area of a bounding region minus an unshaded strip.

KeyConcepts.Title: Expression-to-diagram reasoning
KeyConcepts.Definition: A valid area expression represents the actual selected shaded region and its dimensions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Numerically equal products need not correspond to the same partition or source diagram.
KeyConcepts.Example: Both 8+3 and 12−1 equal 11, but represent different splits.

WorkedExamples.Title: Add a fractional strip
WorkedExamples.Question: Compute the area of a 4-by-2 3/4 shaded rectangle.
WorkedExamples.Method: Build an original unit-area model, then justify the arithmetic.
Steps: Draw a height-4 region with width 2.
Add a separate height-4 by width-3/4 strip.

WorkedExamples.Title: Subtract an unshaded strip
WorkedExamples.Question: A 4-by-3 rectangle has a 1/4-unit-wide unshaded strip. What shaded area remains?
WorkedExamples.Method: Build an original unit-area model, then justify the arithmetic.
Steps: Find full area 4×3=12 square units.
Find omitted strip area 4×1/4=1 square unit.
Subtract 12−1.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject a false match
WorkedExamples.Question: Does 4×(2+1/4) represent either previous 11-square-unit shaded region?
WorkedExamples.Method: Build an original unit-area model, then justify the arithmetic.
Steps: Identify width 2+1/4=2 1/4.
Multiply by height 4 to obtain 9.
Compare 9 with the required shaded 11 square units.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No; the expression represents 9 square units.
WorkedExamples.Check: The expression's width is 1/2 unit shorter than the area-11 width 2 3/4.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Add an unshaded region as though it were colored
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It confuses linear lengths, equal-area partitions, or square-area quantities.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Subtract areas that are physically absent from the shaded model.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claim matching expressions must show the same physical partition
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It confuses linear lengths, equal-area partitions, or square-area quantities.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Different decompositions may have equal totals; justify their own corresponding diagrams separately.

SummaryPoints: Distribute multiplication across plus and minus to match geometric regions.
A correct expression must match actual shaded and unshaded parts, not just a result.
Card sorts and explanation-rich matching remain teacher-reviewed.
